blocks.text: Fertilisers are chemicals that provide essential nutrients to plants to promote growth and increase crop yields. They replenish depleted soil, boost healthy growth and ensure better food production. Synthetic fertilisers are man-made by chemical processes such as the Haber-Bosch process for ammonia (NH3); organic fertilisers come from natural sources such as compost or animal manure.

Plants need essential elements as micronutrients and macronutrients. The micronutrients listed are boron, iron, copper, chlorine, manganese, molybdenum and zinc. The macronutrients are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur, potassium, calcium and magnesium. Of these nine, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are needed in such large amounts that they are called primary macronutrients. Commercial fertilisers are labelled with an N-P-K ratio, which gives the content of these three elements.

blocks.title: Sixteen listed, seventeen stated
blocks.text: The book says plants need seventeen essential elements but lists sixteen (seven micronutrients and nine macronutrients). The element usually counted as the seventeenth is nickel, a micronutrient. Flagged for review.

items: Nitrogen is often the most limiting factor in crop production. It is part of amino acids, which build proteins, and of chlorophyll, the pigment for photosynthesis.
Phosphorus is usually supplied as superphosphates or ammonium phosphates. It is part of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which stores and releases energy.
Potassium, unlike nitrogen and phosphorus, does not become part of the plant's structure. It acts as an osmoregulator and activates over sixty enzymes that help plant metabolism.

blocks.text: Plant roots take up these chemicals. But if too much is used, the excess can wash into rivers and lakes and cause an overgrowth of algae, which harms aquatic life. Long-term use of some synthetic fertilisers can also change the soil's pH and kill useful microorganisms, hurting soil health.

Middle: three cards: N, part of amino acids and chlorophyll; P, supplied as superphosphates or ammonium phosphates, part of ATP; K, an osmoregulator that activates over sixty enzymes. blocks.long_description: Plants need many elements, but nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are needed in the largest amounts, which is why fertiliser labels give their N-P-K ratio.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Why do farmers rotate crops? Growing the same crop every year uses up the same nutrients. Crop rotation restores soil nutrients and reduces the need for synthetic fertilisers.

blocks.prompt: Which N-P-K nutrient promotes protein synthesis and chlorophyll formation?
blocks.explanation: Nitrogen: it is part of amino acids (proteins) and of chlorophyll.

items: Fertilisers supply nutrients; synthetic (Haber-Bosch NH3) or organic (compost, manure).
Primary macronutrients N, P, K; N-P-K label.
Excess: algal overgrowth, soil pH change.
